analysis.one_liner: Restores canceled Arctic Refuge oil leases and blocks courts from reviewing drilling permits.
analysis.headline: The bill, pushed by Alaska's two Republican senators, drew 2 cosponsors and died in the Senate Energy and Natural Resources Committee without ever getting a hearing or a vote.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would force the Interior Department to hand back oil and gas leases in the Arctic National Wildlife Refuge that were canceled, hold a new lease sale, and make it nearly impossible to cancel future leases. It would declare that the 2020 environmental review already satisfies the nation's environmental laws and would strip courts of the power to review drilling approvals — leaving only the oil companies holding the leases able to go to court.
analysis.who_benefits: Oil and gas companies that bid in the January 2021 Arctic Refuge lease sale would get their canceled leases reissued within 30 days of enactment, with the government required to accept the bids as-is [S2][S3]. They and future leaseholders would be shielded: the President and Interior could not cancel a lease once bids were opened unless the holder violated its terms, and no court could review the permits, environmental reviews, or wildlife findings behind the drilling program — with one narrow exception letting leaseholders themselves petition a court to force faster agency action [S2][S3]. Alaska's state government also gains, since it shares in federal drilling revenue and its own development authority bought refuge tracts in the 2021 sale [S3].
analysis.who_benefits_short: Oil companies holding Arctic Refuge leases

how_it_helps.text: Within 30 days of enactment, Interior would have to accept the highest valid January 2021 bids for six canceled lease tracts and reissue the leases without modification, declaring the underlying 2020 approvals fully compliant with the Alaska lands act, NEPA, the Endangered Species Act, and administrative law.

Interior would be required to hold a second Arctic Refuge lease sale by December 22, 2024, and the President and Interior would be barred from canceling any lease once bids were opened unless the holder breaks its terms and fails to cure the violation.

The bill would wipe out every order or action that pauses or suspends Coastal Plain leasing, ratify all permits and wildlife approvals issued under the program, nullify Section 4 of Executive Order 13990 and Secretarial Order 3401 (the 2021 leasing halt), and direct agencies to keep those approvals in force.

It would withdraw the draft supplemental environmental review and the proposed rule for the National Petroleum Reserve in Alaska, and would bar any court from reviewing drilling approvals — including lawsuits already pending — while giving leaseholders a 90-day fast track to force agencies to act in their favor.

analysis.who_pays: The public would bear the cost if the bill passed: the protected coastal plain of a national wildlife refuge would be committed to drilling with environmental reviews declared satisfied by statute and judicial review stripped, so citizens — including Alaska Native communities that depend on the refuge's caribou herds — would have no way to challenge permits in court, even for lawsuits already filed. Future Congresses and presidents would lose their authority to cancel leases in what is supposed to be publicly managed land.
analysis.who_pays_short: The public, via the Arctic Refuge and its courts

drawbacks.text: The judicial-review preclusion is sweeping: no court could review any approval for the drilling program, including lawsuits pending on enactment day, and the only forum left to anyone is the leaseholders' own petition to compel agency action — ordinary citizens, conservation groups, and affected communities would lose their day in court.

By statute declaring that the 2020 environmental record satisfies NEPA, the Endangered Species Act, and administrative law, the bill would remove the normal judicial check even if that analysis was flawed — a heavier-handed fix than the problem it names, and one supporters must acknowledge goes well beyond simply reinstating leases.

It would kill two public rulemaking processes midstream — the draft supplemental environmental review for the Coastal Plain program and the proposed National Petroleum Reserve in Alaska management rule — without letting the public comment process run its course.

The bill's stated rationale is that Congress mandated the leasing program in the 2017 Tax Cuts and Jobs Act and that Interior's lease cancellations exceeded the Secretary's delegated authority; even accepting that argument, the bill resolves the dispute by declaring environmental laws satisfied rather than by re-examining the drilling program's merits.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefits are real but narrow: reissued leases, a guaranteed second sale, and revenue for Alaska's resource economy and the handful of companies that bid in 2021. The costs are broad: a national wildlife refuge opened to drilling with environmental laws deemed satisfied by statute, two public rulemakings canceled, and court access removed for everyone except the leaseholders. An honest supporter gets the leases back at the price of an unusually sweeping court-stripping provision that would set a precedent for Congress deciding environmental compliance by declaration.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced and referred to the Senate Energy and Natural Resources Committee, which never held a hearing, markup, or vote before Congress ended.

narrative.text: Senator Dan Sullivan introduced the bill on November 9, 2023, on behalf of himself and Senator Lisa Murkowski; it was read twice and referred to the Committee on Energy and Natural Resources.
Two Republican senators cosponsored it — 2 of the Senate's 49 Republicans — and no Democratic senator signed on.

The action history ends there: the committee, led by Democrats, took no further action, and the bill received no hearing, no markup, no floor vote, and no companion action before the 118th Congress ended on January 3, 2025.

Because it never became law, none of its provisions took effect: the canceled refuge leases stayed canceled, the leasing pause stood, and the draft environmental review and Petroleum Reserve rule remained subject to the normal agency process.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: The Arctic National Wildlife Refuge's coastal plain stayed shielded from forced leasing, and the public kept its ability to challenge drilling approvals in court. The companies and the Alaska state development authority that lost the 2021 leases in the cancellations did not get them back.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: The Arctic Refuge and its defenders

for.name: Dan Sullivan
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and led its promotion

against.name: Senate Energy and Natural Resources Committee
against.role: Committee of referral, chaired by a Democrat
against.what_they_did: Received the bill on referral and took no further action — no hearing, markup, or vote — for the rest of the Congress

against.name: Conservation groups and Alaska Native subsistence advocates
against.what_they_did: Long-standing opposition to drilling in the refuge's coastal plain, cited in the broader debate over the program the bill would revive

sides.party_line_note: Sponsorship was entirely Republican — Alaska's two GOP senators plus 2 of 49 Senate Republicans — and the Democratic-led committee never acted on it, so support ran on party lines though no votes were ever taken.

industries.industry: Oil and gas companies exploring the Arctic
industries.note: The bill would hand these companies canceled refuge leases within 30 days, guarantee them a second lease sale, and make it nearly impossible to cancel their leases — all while removing the courts from any review of their permits. The gain comes directly out of public control over a national wildlife refuge.

industries.industry: State of Alaska and its development authorities
industries.note: Alaska shares in revenue from the Coastal Plain leasing program created by the 2017 tax law, and a state development authority bought refuge tracts in the 2021 sale, so the bill would restore both the leases and the revenue stream. The gain accrues to the state's resource economy rather than to the refuge's other users.
